title: New Report Opens the 'Black Box' of Fertility Culture
author: Lyman Stone, Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Jason S. Carroll
summary: Lyman Stone, Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Jason Carroll introduce the IFS/Wheatley report Baby Nudges, which tries to specify what 'culture' means when it is used to explain why some groups have many more children than others. Using a survey of nearly 10,000 people in over a dozen countries and a database of the family lives of historic and current public figures, they test how peers, parents, celebrities and religious communities shape fertility desires. Their six findings include that supportive friends and parents raise fertility intentions, that admired public figures with larger families raise intentions, and that active faith matters mainly through community encouragement. They also report that belief in a moral obligation to have children predicts little, while seeing children as a joy does, and that the division of household labor has little effect. The authors call the work an experiment that barely scratches the surface.
points: 'Culture' is too often a catch-all label for whatever fertility variation other variables fail to explain, so the report tries to isolate specific attitudes.
Feeling supported by friends and encouraged by parents is associated with wanting, intending and having more children.
Admiring a public figure with a larger family is associated with a 14% increase in the likelihood of intending another child.
Positive attitudes toward family life, not a felt moral obligation, predict fertility intentions, and household labor division shows little effect.
Religious attendance relates to higher fertility mostly through community support and encouragement, not through pro-family statements from leaders.
quotes: These contrasting trends highlight how people inhabiting similar economic worlds end up with radically different families.

Unfortunately, “culture” has long been used as a catch-all term: any variation in fertility not explained by variables we understand well (like housing costs, contraception, child mortality, or marriage rates) too often ends up lumped together as “culture.

When people feel supported by friends, they desire, intend to have, and actually have more children. Likewise, when people feel encouraged to have children by their parents, they also desire and intend to have more children.

Admiring a public figure with a family bigger than one's own is associated with a 14% increase in the likelihood of intending another child, and changes in cultural elites’ fertility or visible fertility have historically predicted changes in populations’ fertility.

Belief that most people have a moral obligation to have children does not significantly predict intent to have a child, but beliefs that children are the greatest joy or represent the future of one's community does.

Contrary to theories that low fertility may be due to unequal sharing of domestic labor, neither actual division of household chores nor perceptions around their fairness significantly predict any meaningful differences in fertility ideals or intentions.

However, this association is not driven by the frequency of pro-family statements from religious leaders but is more likely due to greater support and encouragement from family and other religious community members.

High levels of “safety-ism,” general anxiety, and pessimism about the future are all strong candidates for cultural changes that are driving falling fertility today, since other research has shown that these may be rising over time.
